Overview

Santiago as a Business Centre

Santiago is Chile's capital and its economic centre. INE's first 2024 census results put the Santiago Metropolitan Region at 7,400,741 people, about 40 percent of the national population. Regional output is led by financial and business services, commerce, personal services, real estate and manufacturing, according to Central Bank figures compiled by the Library of the National Congress. Most of the country's banks, pension fund managers, insurers, listed companies and law firms are based in the city, together with the head offices of mining, energy, retail and forestry groups whose operations lie elsewhere in Chile. The Central Bank, the Financial Market Commission and the Santiago Stock Exchange are all in the city, as are the Supreme Court and the largest court of appeals.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Santiago because Chilean deals and disputes are mostly negotiated, financed and decided there, even when the mine, power plant or project is hundreds of kilometres away. Foreign investors and lenders need background on business groups, families and executives that control Chilean companies through layered holding structures. Construction, infrastructure and real estate projects bring contractor and counterparty risk, and these sectors dominate the caseload at the city's main arbitration centre. Creditors need to find assets recorded in Santiago's registries. And in a market with strong institutions but concentrated ownership, conflicts of interest and related-party dealings are common questions in pre-transaction reviews.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Santiago

01

Business group and owner diligence

Researching Santiago-based business groups, family holding companies and executives before acquisitions, joint ventures or financing, using commerce registry and company records, CMF filings for regulated issuers, court records and Spanish-language media, and mapping control through layered holding structures.

02

Construction and real estate disputes

Supporting counsel in construction, infrastructure and real estate disputes, the largest categories at CAM Santiago, with background on contractors, developers and their owners, research into related companies and prior disputes, and identification of assets relevant to recovery.

03

Mining and energy counterparty reviews

Reviewing Santiago-headquartered suppliers, contractors, consultants and project partners in mining and energy for ownership, links to officials or competitors, sanctions and adverse media, and capability, before contract award or investment in projects located elsewhere in Chile.

04

Asset research for creditors

Identifying real property, company interests, vehicles and other assets of judgment or award debtors through Santiago's property and commerce registries and related records, so that counsel can plan precautionary measures and enforcement before the Santiago courts or in recognition proceedings.

05

Internal fraud and conflict inquiries

Assisting companies with Santiago offices where fraud, kickbacks, undisclosed related-party transactions or conflicts of interest are suspected, scoping document review, interviews and background research with Chilean counsel so that findings can support disciplinary, civil or criminal steps.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Santiago

Courts sitting in Santiago

The Supreme Court of Chile sits in Santiago, as does the Santiago Court of Appeals, the country's busiest, which reviews first-instance civil judgments and hears challenges to arbitral awards. Chile has no separate commercial courts; commercial and contract disputes are heard by the civil courts of Santiago. Recognition of foreign judgments and awards is decided by the Supreme Court. Court files are largely accessible through the judiciary's online system, which helps litigation and background research.

CAM Santiago

The Centro de Arbitraje y Mediación of the Santiago Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1992, administers domestic arbitration, international arbitration since 2006, mediation and dispute boards. It has received 7,796 requests since its founding. In the first half of 2026, real estate, construction and infrastructure and commercial companies led its domestic caseload, and 75.4 percent of court challenges to its awards were rejected. Law 19.971 governs international commercial arbitration in Chile.

Conservador and commerce registries

The Conservador de Bienes Raíces de Santiago keeps the property registry for the city's communes within its territory, recording ownership, mortgages and encumbrances, and also maintains the Commerce Registry where many company constitutions and amendments are recorded. Certificates are generally available on request. Companies formed under the simplified online system appear in the national Registro de Empresas y Sociedades. Both are core sources for ownership and asset research.

Financial regulators and exchange

The Comisión para el Mercado Financiero, which supervises securities, insurance and banking, and the Central Bank of Chile are based in Santiago, as is the Santiago Stock Exchange. CMF filings and sanction resolutions are public and are a key source on listed companies, their controllers and executives. Chile's private security law of 2024, in force since 2025, is administered nationally; its application to investigative consulting is checked with Chilean counsel.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Santiago

TDSC handles Santiago matters from Nashville and has no office, staff or licence in Chile. Engagements start by setting out which sources apply: Conservador property and commerce certificates, company registry data, CMF filings and sanction resolutions, Santiago court files available through the judiciary's online system, and Spanish-language media and open sources. Where interviews, site visits or local inquiries are needed, TDSC coordinates qualified Chilean professionals and agrees the method with the client's Chilean counsel, with attention to the private security law, criminal-law limits on recording in private spaces and Chile's data protection reforms. Reports prepared for CAM Santiago arbitrations or court proceedings separate documented facts from inference.

TDSC has no office in Santiago. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Santiago: Frequently Asked Questions

Where are property and company records held in Santiago?

The Conservador de Bienes Raíces de Santiago keeps the property registry and the Commerce Registry for its territory, and certificates of ownership, encumbrances and company records can generally be requested. Companies formed through the simplified online system are recorded in the national Registro de Empresas y Sociedades. Research usually combines both with CMF and court records.

Which arbitral institution is used in Santiago?

The main institution is CAM Santiago, the arbitration and mediation centre of the Santiago Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1992 and administering international cases since 2006. Real estate, construction and infrastructure disputes dominate its caseload. TDSC does not advise on institution choice but supports research for Santiago-seated proceedings.

Are Santiago court files publicly accessible?

Many Chilean court files can be consulted through the judiciary's online system, which makes litigation history a valuable source in background research. Access varies by matter type, and some proceedings, such as family matters, are restricted. TDSC uses only lawfully accessible records and notes where files could not be reviewed.

Does Chile have commercial courts in Santiago?

Chile does not have separate commercial courts. Commercial disputes in Santiago are heard by the civil courts, with appeals to the Santiago Court of Appeals and ultimately the Supreme Court. Many larger commercial contracts instead provide for arbitration, often at CAM Santiago. Forum strategy is a matter for Chilean counsel.

Why research business groups before investing in Chile?

Many Chilean companies are controlled by family business groups through several layers of holding companies, and decisions are taken in Santiago. Understanding who controls a counterparty, its related companies and its executives' other interests helps investors identify conflicts of interest and related-party risk before committing capital.
